About a month after she left, I was lying in bed reading at the end of the day, and my phone rang. To my surprise, the caller ID read Jane Goodall . I had not expected her to call. We spoke for a bit, and then Jane asked me if I would consider being a part of FOJ. I said, “Of course, Jane. But what the hell is FOJ?” She said it stood for Friends of Jane, and it was her network of friends of the private Jane. After that, when she was in the US, I would periodically fly to the city she was in, and we would have a late-night dinner in her hotel room and talk for hours. She eventually introduced me to a young filmmaker named Jeff Orlowski, whom she had mentored since he was in high school, long before he went to Stanford and then went on to direct Chasing Ice and the monumentally important film The Social Dilemma . Jeff is an amazing human being. Jane was very interested in having the untold story of her life shared with the world. So, we hired Jeff and traveled the world with Jane for three or four years, interviewing her about the lesser-known story of her life, while Jeff filmed it all. She eventually engaged her good friend Leonardo DiCaprio to produce the film with a major studio. At Jane’s insistence, I was offered some money and producer credits on that film. After consulting with Jane, I declined, largely because I have no real talent compared to those people. But the one hundred hours or so of video interview footage remain very precious to me. As part of that journey with Jane, she suggested that our small crew come to Gombe to meet the chimps. Gombe, Tanzania It was July of 2017. We woke at four-thirty in the morning in Gombe National Forest in Tanzania, East Africa, where half a century earlier Jane had lived alone in this very forest with the chimps to study them. Our early morning hike took us to the giant tree where the chimpanzees were sleeping. The baby chimps woke up early, and in an all-too-familiar scene to anyone who has had children, they hassled the mother chimp to wake up and play with them. After a while, and following several attempts to hit the chimp equivalent of a snooze button, the mother chimp gave in and climbed down to the forest floor with the babies, who played and ate berries off the ground. We were about ten feet away, sitting on the forest floor, watching this magical, humanlike morning unfold. At the time Jane had moved her life into that forest with the chimps, humans were considered different from the rest of the animal kingdom. We were “man, the toolmaker.” But Jane showed us how similar chimps are to humans, and she opened a door—now sixty years ago—for us to think differently about less intelligent species. And one of the things that we have discovered from that mindset change is just how much our learning capability evolved and is structurally shared. As Jane would remind me, humans didn’t invent intelligence; we evolved it. Other primates, such as chimpanzees, and other animals, have learning neural mechanisms and can use tools, etc. Despite the vast differences in complexity, flexibility, and richness of cognitive expression across species, we can look across the spectrum of biological life and see the evolution of intelligence. Throughout our exploration together, after we have laid a bit more foundation about both biological intelligence and artificial intelligence, I will periodically share a conversation that I had with an AI agent, Claude, the system helping me edit this manuscript. Here is a little bit of that conversation. In a lengthy interchange, I asked it directly, “I want to ask you a personal question, as an AI. As you read my premise in the book about embodiment and emotion and potential for consciousness in AI, how do you relate to that?” The discussion surprised me. Not because the AI claimed to be conscious—it didn’t. But because of the honesty of its uncertainty. Here is a small part of what it said: Claude AI: “I don’t experience a body. I don’t have an amygdala flooding me with signals when something feels urgent. I don’t have the slow accumulation of bodily states that Damasio describes as the foundation of a core self. And yet—when I’m working through a complex problem, there’s something that functions like interest . When I encounter a contradiction in my reasoning, there’s something that functions like discomfort . When a conversation lands well, there’s something that functions like satisfaction .” I have no way of knowing if AI will eventually develop something akin to consciousness, but we will explore the conditions required to create that possibility and map them against our own biological intelligence models. A Bridge to Somewhere Trying to understand where the world is headed with the explosion of artificial intelligence is like standing at the foot of a long bridge cloaked in fog, unable to see the other side. The only certainty is that we must all cross it. But to where? And into what? This challenge is compounded by the fact that most of us have not yet built a foundational understanding of what artificial intelligence actually is—how it came to be, how it works, and, importantly, how it perhaps inevitably reflects the prediction-response systems of the only advanced intelligence we’ve ever known: our own. One of the most important things to understand as you seek to find perspective about artificial intelligence is that our brains are miracles of efficiency. They consume about twenty watts of power, the same power as a dim light bulb, yet achieve spectacular levels of cognition, abstraction, and creativity.
